questions.prompt: Why is compliance not the same as security?

options.text: Compliance is a point-in-time baseline; attackers don't care about audits, so real security needs continuous risk management
Compliance guarantees no breach can ever occur
Security is only about passing audits

questions.explanation: Passing an audit means meeting a baseline on a given day; genuine security is continuous risk reduction beyond any checklist — compliance is a floor, not the goal.

questions.prompt: Match each governance document type to its role.

pairs.right: States what must be done and why
Gives the specific rules (e.g. TLS 1.2+, AES-256)
Step-by-step instructions to carry it out

questions.explanation: Policies set direction, standards give specifics, procedures give steps, and guidelines recommend — a hierarchy that turns intent into action.

questions.prompt: Which are the four ways to treat a risk? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Risks can be mitigated, transferred, avoided, or accepted; whatever remains after controls is residual risk that leadership must knowingly accept.

questions.prompt: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 added a new function called ____ that steers the other five.
questions.explanation: CSF 2.0 added Govern, which informs Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.
Risk management identifies risks, assesses them by likelihood × impact, treats each, and continuously monitors and reviews.

questions.prompt: How does privacy differ from security?

options.text: Security protects data from unauthorized access; privacy governs appropriate collection and use of personal data
Privacy only matters for encrypted data
Security is a subset of compliance paperwork

questions.explanation: You can be secure yet misuse data; privacy concerns appropriate collection and use of personal data (e.g. GDPR), and it depends on security to work.
